sections.title: Stretching, compressing or bending needs more than one force

parts.title: Why two forces
parts.html:
A force changes an object's motion or its shape. With one force there is a resultant, so the object as a whole accelerates (Topic 2) — it moves off rather than stretching. To distort it (stretch, compress or bend it) you need more than one force: forces in different directions that between them pull the parts of the object apart, push them together, or turn them. Pull both ends of a spring outward and it stretches; push both ends inward and it compresses; push the middle of a ruler one way while its ends are held the other way and it bends.

The second force is usually supplied by whatever the object is attached to or resting on: the hook pulls up on a hanging spring while the weight pulls down; the table pushes up on a sponge you press; the wall pushes back on a ball thrown at it. In the exam, name both: "the weight of the mass pulls the bottom of the spring down and the clamp pulls the top up, so the spring is stretched".

parts.title: Naming both forces
parts.question: A student hangs a mass from a spring attached to a clamp. Explain why the spring stretches rather than simply moving downwards. (2 marks)
steps: The weight of the mass pulls the bottom of the spring down, and the clamp pulls the top up — two forces in opposite directions.
With a force at each end the spring cannot accelerate as a whole (the forces balance), so instead it changes shape: it stretches. One force alone would just accelerate it.

questions.text: Explain why you cannot stretch a spring by pulling on one end only. (2)
questions.model:
• Pulling one end gives a single, unbalanced force: a resultant.
  • A resultant force accelerates the spring as a whole; to stretch it the other end must be held or pulled the other way, so that there are two forces in opposite directions.

questions.text: A sponge is squashed on a table. The two forces that compress it are…
options: your hand pushing down and the table pushing up
questions.explain: The table supplies the second force.

questions.text: Name the three ways an object can be distorted, and give an everyday example of each. (3)
questions.model:
• Stretching — a spring or elastic band pulled at both ends.
  • Compression — a sponge or car spring squashed between two forces.
  • Bending — a ruler or diving board pushed in the middle while its ends are held (or held at one end and pushed at the other).

questions.text: A ball is thrown at a wall and squashes slightly on impact. The second force that compresses it is…
options: the push of the wall on the ball
questions.explain: The back of the ball keeps moving forward while the wall pushes the front of the ball back: two forces.

questions.text: An object with a single force acting on it…
questions.explain: One force is a resultant force.

checklist: Explain why a single force cannot stretch, compress or bend an object
Identify both forces in a stretching, squashing or bending situation
Describe the three kinds of distortion: stretching, compression, bending
sections.blurb: To change the shape of an object you need at least two forces acting on it in different directions. One force on its own gives a resultant, and a resultant force accelerates the whole object instead of distorting it. The second force is often the one you forget: the hook holding the spring, the wall behind the ball, the table under the ruler.

sections.title: Elastic and inelastic distortion

parts.title: Does it go back?
parts.html:
Elastic distortionInelastic distortion
Definitionthe object returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removedthe object does not return to its original shape: it is permanently distorted
Examplesa spring within its elastic limit, an elastic band, a rubber ball, a diving board, a car's springsmodelling clay, a crushed can, a bent paperclip, a spring stretched too far (it stays longer)
Energythe work done stretching it is stored (elastic potential energy) and given back as it returnsthe work done goes into rearranging the material and is not recovered

The elastic limit is the point beyond which the distortion stops being elastic: stretch a spring past it and it will not return to its original length. Up to the elastic limit the extension is also proportional to the force (Hooke's law, N3) for a spring — strictly the straight line ends at the limit of proportionality, just before the elastic limit, but for a GCSE spring the two are treated as the same point. The examiners' word is distortion (not "deformation", though that is accepted) and the two kinds are elastic and inelastic, not "plastic".

parts.title: Two springs
parts.question: Two identical springs are loaded. Spring A returns to 5.0 cm when unloaded; spring B stays at 6.2 cm. Explain the difference. (2 marks)
steps: Spring A was distorted elastically: it returned to its original length when the force was removed, so it was not stretched beyond its elastic limit.
Spring B was stretched beyond its elastic limit, so its distortion was inelastic: it is permanently longer.

questions.text: State what is meant by an elastic distortion. (1)
questions.model: • A change of shape that is reversed when the forces are removed — the object returns to its original shape and size.

questions.text: Which is an inelastic distortion?
options: A squashed drinks can staying squashed
An elastic band returning to size
A diving board returning to level
questions.explain: Permanent change = inelastic.

questions.text: A spring is stretched and does not return to its original length. State what has happened and why. (2)
questions.model:
• It has been distorted inelastically (permanently).
  • Because it was stretched beyond its elastic limit.

questions.text: The elastic limit of a spring is…
options: the force at which it snaps
the point beyond which it no longer returns to its original length when unloaded
questions.explain: Beyond it, the distortion is inelastic.

questions.text: Which word do the mark schemes use for a change of shape?
questions.explain: Elastic distortion / inelastic distortion.

checklist: Define elastic distortion and inelastic distortion
State what the elastic limit is
Give examples of materials that behave elastically and inelastically
sections.blurb: An elastic distortion is undone when the forces are removed — the spring goes back to its original length. An inelastic distortion stays: the object is permanently changed. Every spring is elastic up to its elastic limit and inelastic beyond it.

sections.title: Hooke's law: force, extension and the spring constant

parts.title: The equation and its trap
parts.html:
Hooke's law: the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. As an equation, $F = k x$: force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m). The spring constant $k$ is the force needed for each metre of extension — a measure of stiffness. A car suspension spring might be 50 000 N/m; a lab spring 25 N/m. The same equation describes a compression: $x$ is then how much shorter the spring is.

$x$ is the extension — the change in length, stretched length − original length — not the length. The June 2023 scheme (Q7(a)(ii)) gave three marks for exactly this: read the position of the top of the spring against the ruler, read it again when pressed down, subtract the two readings. And it must be in metres when $k$ is in N/m: the June 2025 report (Q8(b)(ii)) saw candidates "use the extension in cm and give the value as N/m", which was "100 times too small" and scored one mark of two. 6.2 mm is $6.2 \times 10^{-3}$ m; 4 cm is 0.04 m.

parts.title: A compressed spring
parts.question: A spring in a stapler has a spring constant of 260 N/m. It is compressed by 6.2 mm. Calculate the force on the spring. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (3 marks)
steps: $F = 1.6$ N (2 s.f.) — the June 2023 Q7(a)(i) marks were selection and substitution, evaluation, and the 2 s.f. answer; 1600 N (mm not converted) earned two of the three.

questions.text: A spring of spring constant 60 N/m is stretched by 25 cm. Calculate the force applied.
A spring is 8.0 cm long with no load and 11.0 cm long with a 6.0 N weight hanging from it. Calculate its spring constant.
A force of 12 N compresses a spring of spring constant 300 N/m. Calculate the compression in mm.
A spring is 12 cm long unstretched and 20 cm long when loaded with 4 N. A student writes $k = 4 \div 0.20 = 20$ N/m. The mistake is…
options: the force should be in kN
the length was used instead of the extension (8 cm = 0.08 m, so $k = 50$ N/m)
the answer should be in N/cm
questions.explain: Extension = loaded length − unloaded length.

questions.text: A spring constant of 500 N/m means…
options: a force of 500 N would stretch the spring by 1 m (within its limit): 5 N per cm
500 N is needed for any extension
questions.explain: Force per metre of extension — stiffness.

checklist: Use $F = kx$ to find force, extension or spring constant
Use the extension (change in length), never the length, and convert cm or mm to m
Explain what the spring constant tells you and give its unit
sections.blurb: For a spring within its limit, the force is proportional to the extension: $F = kx$. The spring constant $k$ is the force per metre of extension, so a stiff spring has a large k. The equation is on the list; the marks are lost on x — it is the extension, not the length, and it must be in metres for k in N/m.

sections.title: The energy stored in a stretched spring

parts.title: Work done stretching
parts.html:
The work done stretching a spring (within its limit) is stored as elastic potential energy: $E = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$, energy (J) = ½ × spring constant (N/m) × extension² (m²). Why ½? Work = force × distance (Topic 8), but the force is not constant: it starts at zero and rises to $F = kx$ as the spring stretches, so the average force is $\tfrac{1}{2} k x$ and the work is $\tfrac{1}{2} k x \times x$. On a force–extension graph that is the area of the triangle under the straight line, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times F \times x$ — the same number.

Two traps. Convert the extension to metres first: 10 cm squared is $0.10^2 = 0.010$ m², not 100 — the June 2025 report (Q8(b)(i), the area $\tfrac{1}{2} F x$ with $x$ left in cm) saw answers "100 times too large"; with $\tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$ the slip is squared, 10 000 times. And it is $x^2$, so doubling the extension quadruples the energy. The energy is returned when the spring is released (an elastic distortion): a catapult turns it into kinetic energy, a pogo stick into gravitational potential energy.

parts.title: Energy in a stretched spring
parts.question: A spring with a spring constant of 80 N/m is stretched by 25 cm. Calculate the energy stored in it. (3 marks)
steps: $E = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.25^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.0625$.

questions.text: A spring of spring constant 150 N/m is compressed by 4.0 cm. Calculate the energy stored.
A spring is stretched by 0.30 m and stores 9.0 J. Calculate its spring constant.
A toy launcher's spring has a spring constant of 160 N/m and is compressed by 0.25 m. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy it could give a ball.
questions.hint: All the stored energy becomes KE.

questions.text: The extension of a spring is doubled (within its limit). The energy stored…
questions.explain: $E \propto x^2$.

questions.text: A student finds $E = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 10^2 = 2500$ J for a spring stretched by 10 cm. The answer is…
options: 10 000 times too large: 10 cm = 0.10 m, so $E = 0.25$ J
questions.explain: The extension must be squared in metres.

checklist: Use $E = 	frac{1}{2} k x^2$ to find the energy stored (or work done) in stretching a spring
Square the extension in metres, not in centimetres
Explain why the energy is the area under a force–extension graph
sections.blurb: Stretching a spring does work on it, and the work is stored as elastic potential energy: $E = 	frac{1}{2} k x^2$. The ½ is there because the force grows from zero as the spring stretches, so the average force is half the final force — which is why the energy is also the area under the force–extension line.

sections.title: Linear and non-linear force–extension graphs
equations: \text{straight line through the origin: } F \propto x

parts.title: Reading the shape
parts.html:
Linear (a straight line through the origin): force is directly proportional to extension — double the force, double the extension — and the gradient of force against extension is the spring constant $k$. This is the region where Hooke's law applies. Non-linear (a curve): the extension is no longer proportional to the force. For a spring the curve begins at the limit of proportionality; beyond it each extra newton stretches the spring by more than before (the line bends towards the extension axis), and a little further on is the elastic limit, after which the spring will not return.

Two things to say in words: "a straight line through the origin, so force is proportional to extension" (both parts — a straight line that does not pass through the origin is not proportional); and "beyond point P the graph is non-linear, so the spring no longer obeys Hooke's law". The graph can be drawn either way up: with extension on the $y$-axis the gradient is $1/k$, and the curve bends upwards past the limit. Check the axes before reading a gradient. A rubber band gives a curve from the start (and a different curve unloading) — it does not obey Hooke's law at all.

parts.title: Describing the graph
parts.question: The graph shows force against extension for a spring. Describe the relationship shown, and find the spring constant. (4 marks)
steps: Up to 8 cm the graph is a straight line through the origin: force is directly proportional to extension (Hooke's law applies).
Beyond 8 cm (the limit of proportionality, 16 N) the graph is non-linear — it curves — so the extension is no longer proportional to the force and each extra newton gives more extension.
Spring constant = gradient of the straight part: $k = 16 \div 0.080$ (8 cm in metres).

graph.alt: Force against extension for a spring: a straight line through the origin up to 8 cm and 16 N, then a curve that bends over towards 20 N at 12 cm.

questions.text: Use the force–extension graph.

parts.text: Use the graph to find the extension when the force is 12 N.
parts.hint: Read across from 12 N to the straight line.
walkthrough: On the straight line, 12 N is at an extension of 6 cm.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the spring at an extension of 6.0 cm.
parts.hint: Area of the triangle under the line up to 6 cm (force 12 N), with x in metres.
walkthrough: at 6.0 cm the force is 12 N; $x = 0.060$ m
parts.label: b

parts.text: Which statement about the part of the graph beyond 8 cm is correct?
options: Force is still proportional to extension
Each extra newton of force produces a larger extension than before; Hooke's law no longer applies
parts.explain: Non-linear: the line bends towards the extension axis.
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Force against extension for a spring: a straight line through the origin up to 8 cm and 16 N, then a curve that bends over towards 20 N at 12 cm.

questions.text: A student plots extension against force for a spring and gets a straight line through the origin. State what this shows about the relationship, and how the spring constant is found from the graph. (2)
questions.model:
• Extension is directly proportional to force (Hooke's law): a straight line through the origin.
  • With extension on the $y$-axis the gradient is $1 \div k$, so $k = 1 \div$ gradient (or read a pair of values and use $k = F \div x$).

questions.text: A force–extension graph is a straight line that does NOT pass through the origin. Force is…
options: not proportional to extension (a linear relationship, but not a proportional one)
questions.explain: Proportional needs the line through the origin.

checklist: Describe a linear force–extension relationship and what it shows
Identify the limit of proportionality on a graph and describe the non-linear part
Find the spring constant from the gradient of the linear part
sections.blurb: Force against extension for a spring is a straight line through the origin — linear, so force is proportional to extension and the gradient is the spring constant. Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves: the same extra force gives more extension than before, and Hooke's law no longer applies. Rubber bands curve from the start.

sections.title: The spring core practical: extension against force, and the work done

parts.title: The method and its marks
parts.html:
StepWhat to write
Apparatusspring, clamp and stand, metre ruler (mm scale) clamped vertically, slotted masses and hanger, a pointer (a pin or splint fixed to the bottom of the spring), safety glasses
Zero readingwith no load, read the position of the bottom of the spring (the pointer) on the ruler
Loadingadd a 100 g mass (weight 1 N); read the new position; repeat adding one mass at a time, up to about 6 masses
Extensionfor each load, extension = new reading − zero reading (June 2023 Q7(a)(ii): read with no load, read with the load, subtract)
Graphplot force ($W = mg$) against extension; a straight line through the origin confirms Hooke's law; gradient = $k$; the area under the line up to an extension is the work done stretching the spring to it
Accuracyread the ruler at eye level with a pointer to avoid parallax (June 2023 Q7(a)(iii): a change "to enable accurate location of the top of the spring" (the moving end, in that question) and how it is used); ruler vertical and clamped; wait for the spring to stop moving; do not load past the elastic limit (check it returns to the zero reading when unloaded); repeat unloading as well as loading

parts.title: Measuring the extension
parts.question: Describe how a student could measure the extension of a spring when a mass is hung from it. (3 marks)
steps: Clamp a ruler vertically beside the spring and read the position of the bottom of the spring (a pointer) with no load.
Hang the mass on the spring, wait for it to settle, and read the position of the pointer again — reading at eye level each time to avoid parallax.
Extension = loaded reading − unloaded reading (in mm).

questions.text: A student hangs masses on a spring and, for each mass, writes down the length of the spring read from a ruler held in her hand beside it, looking down at the scale from above. She then plots force against length. Give three improvements to her method and say what each improves. (3)
questions.model:
• Clamp the ruler vertically beside the spring (not hand-held), so the readings are from a fixed scale.
  • Read the pointer at eye level (not from above), to avoid parallax error.
  • Record the no-load reading and subtract it from each reading to get the extension, and plot force against extension — Hooke's law is about the extension, so the line should pass through the origin.

questions.text: Why is a pointer fixed to the bottom of the spring?
options: So the position on the ruler can be read accurately at eye level, reducing parallax error
questions.explain: 2023 Q7(a)(iii): a change to locate the end of the spring accurately.

questions.text: The pointer reads 142 mm with no load and 187 mm with 3.0 N hanging. Calculate the spring constant.
Explain how the work done in stretching the spring to a given extension can be found from the force–extension graph. (2)
questions.model:
• Work done = area under the line up to that extension.
  • For the straight part this is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times$ force $\times$ extension (extension in metres), the same as $\tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$.

questions.text: Which precaution checks that the spring has not been stretched beyond its elastic limit?
options: Removing the masses and checking the pointer returns to the zero reading
questions.explain: If it does not return, the last readings were past the limit.

checklist: Describe the method: apparatus, readings, how the extension is found
State the accuracy points: eye level, pointer, zero reading, not past the limit
Use the graph: gradient for k, area for the work done stretching
sections.blurb: Hang a spring from a clamp, note where its end is against a ruler, add masses one at a time and note the new position each time. The extension is the difference; the force is the weight added. Plot force against extension: the gradient is k and the area is the work done. The 2023 marks were for the two readings and the subtraction, and for reading at eye level.

sections.title: Pressure: force per unit area

parts.title: The equation and the explanation
parts.html:
Pressure = force ÷ area, $P = F \div A$, in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²), with the force at right angles to the surface. A force of 800 N on 0.4 m² is 2000 Pa; the same 800 N on 0.0004 m² (the point of a stiletto heel) is 2 000 000 Pa. Large area → small pressure: snowshoes, skis, wide tyres, camel feet, the broad base of a dam, a wide strap. Small area → large pressure: a knife edge, a nail point, a drawing pin, football studs, an ice skate.

The June 2022 report (Q4(a)(ii), why a camel's wide feet help on sand): the marks were for the larger surface area and for less pressure (or the weight spread over a larger area); "the mass spread out" was "unworthy of a second mark" — say force or weight spread over the area, and name the pressure. The same report's Q4(a)(i): a donkey's weight on four hooves — the area in $P = F \div A$ is the total area in contact, 4 × one hoof; forgetting the four cost a mark. And the area must be in m²: 1 cm² = $10^{-4}$ m², 1 mm² = $10^{-6}$ m² (June 2025 Q1(c): an area left in mm² gave "an answer that was a million times too large").

parts.title: Pressure under four feet
parts.question: A donkey weighs 2000 N. Each hoof has an area of 50 cm². Calculate the pressure the donkey exerts on the ground when standing on all four hooves. (3 marks)
steps: Total area $= 4 \times 50 = 200$ cm² $= 200 \times 10^{-4} = 0.020$ m².

questions.text: A box weighs 450 N and its base is 0.30 m by 0.50 m. Calculate the pressure on the floor.
A drawing pin is pushed with a force of 8.0 N. The point has an area of 0.20 mm². Calculate the pressure at the point.
The pressure of the air on a window is 100 000 Pa. The window has an area of 0.80 m². Calculate the force on it.
Explain why a person wearing snowshoes does not sink into soft snow as far as a person in ordinary boots. (2)
questions.model:
• The snowshoes have a much larger area in contact with the snow, so the person's weight is spread over a larger area.
  • Pressure = force ÷ area, so the pressure on the snow is smaller and the snow is not compressed as much.

questions.text: A student explains a camel's wide feet with 'its mass is spread out'. The 2022 examiners…
options: did not credit it: say the weight (force) is spread over a larger area, so the pressure is less
questions.explain: Force, not mass; and name the pressure.

checklist: Use $P = F/A$ to find pressure, force or area
Explain a design in terms of area and pressure, in the words that score
Convert cm² and mm² to m² before substituting
sections.blurb: Pressure is the force per unit area: the same force on a smaller area is a larger pressure. Snowshoes, tractor tyres and camel hooves spread a weight over a large area; a knife edge, a drawing pin and a stiletto heel concentrate it. The equation is on the list; the marks are on the area — all of it, in m².

sections.title: Pressure in a fluid: the fluid plus the atmosphere, acting at right angles to every surface
equations: F = P\,A \text{ normal to the surface}

parts.title: Normal to the surface
parts.html:
A fluid (liquid or gas) has no fixed shape, so its pressure is not in one direction: at any point it pushes equally in all directions, and on any surface it produces a force at right angles — normal — to that surface. On the floor of a tank the force is downward; on a vertical wall, sideways; on a curved submarine hull, inward everywhere, perpendicular to the hull. The June 2023 scheme (Q4(a)(iv), the force of the cabin air on an aeroplane window) wanted the arrow pointing towards the outside and normal to the surface at X; the June 2024 scheme (Q4(a)) asked for the direction "normal to the surface, acting towards the surface". Draw the arrow from the point on the surface, perpendicular to it (2025 Q1(a)(ii): an arrow "too far away from the point" scored nothing).

The total pressure at a depth in a liquid is the pressure due to the liquid plus the atmospheric pressure pressing on its surface (about 100 kPa at sea level). A surface with fluid on both sides feels the difference: the 2023 aeroplane window had 80 kPa inside and 23 kPa outside, so the net pressure was $80\,000 - 23\,000 = 57\,000$ Pa outward, and the force on a 0.094 m² window from the inside was $F = P A = 80\,000 \times 0.094 = 7500$ N. A larger window at the same pressure gets a larger force (Q4(a)(iii): "force is greater on the large window; pressure is the same").

parts.title: The force on a window
parts.question: The air inside an aeroplane cabin is at 80 kPa and the air outside at 23 kPa. (a) Calculate the net pressure on a window. (b) A window has an area of 0.094 m². Calculate the force of the cabin air on it. (3 marks)
steps: (a) net pressure $= 80\,000 - 23\,000 = 57\,000$ Pa, acting outward (the June 2023 Q4(a)(i) answer).
$F = 7500$ N (7520 N), at right angles to the window, towards the outside.

questions.text: The force from the water on the sloping side of a swimming pool acts…
options: at right angles to the sloping side, towards it
questions.explain: Normal to the surface, whatever its angle.

questions.text: The pressure inside a sealed container is 150 kPa and the atmospheric pressure outside is 100 kPa. The lid has an area of 0.020 m². Calculate the net force on the lid.
The pressure at the bottom of a lake is 'due to the water plus the atmosphere'. Explain what this means. (2)
questions.model:
• The water above the point presses down on it — the pressure due to the liquid (which increases with depth).
  • The air above the lake presses down on the water's surface too, so the atmospheric pressure (about 100 kPa) is added to it: total = liquid + atmosphere.

questions.text: Two windows in the same cabin: one large, one small. Compared with the small window, the large one has…
options: a greater force on it and the same pressure
questions.explain: $F = PA$; the pressure is the same everywhere in the cabin.

questions.text: A pressure of $4.8 \times 10^{7}$ Pa acts on a surface of area $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ m². Calculate the force, to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough: Units: N (2 s.f. — the June 2024 Q4(b) third mark was for the rounding)

checklist: State that the pressure in a fluid is due to the fluid and to the atmosphere
Draw the force from a fluid's pressure at right angles to the surface, towards it
Use $F = PA$, including a difference in pressure across a surface
sections.blurb: A fluid is a liquid or a gas. The pressure at a point in a fluid is the pressure due to the fluid itself plus the atmospheric pressure on top of it, and it pushes at right angles (normal) to any surface it touches — walls, floor, a diver, the inside of a window. Force on a surface = pressure × area.

sections.title: Atmospheric pressure, and why it falls with height
equations: \text{less air above} \rightarrow \text{less weight of air} \rightarrow \text{lower pressure}

parts.title: Less air above
parts.html:
Atmospheric pressure is the pressure of the air: the weight of the column of air above a surface, spread over that surface, about 100 kPa (100 000 N on every square metre) at sea level — plus the constant bombardment of air molecules (Topic 14), which is the same thing seen from the particle side. We do not feel it because the fluids inside us push out just as hard.

Why it falls with height: higher up there is less air above you, so a smaller weight of air presses down on each square metre, so the pressure is lower. The air is also less dense higher up — the particles are further apart — because it is not squeezed by as much air above it, and this is why the graph is a curve: each kilometre of thin high air weighs less than a kilometre of dense low air, so the pressure falls by less and less per kilometre. The June 2023 scheme (Q4(b)) gave marks for "increase in height results in decrease in pressure", "non-linear relationship" and "use of numerical data" from the graph, and for the explanation any one of "air becomes less dense", "smaller weight of air above"; the June 2024 scheme (Q4(c)) wanted "as height increases pressure decreases" (a negative correlation) and "non-linear — curved, not proportional, the gradient changes". Gravity getting weaker is not the reason (it barely changes over 10 km): the June 2024 scheme (Q4(d)) said to ignore it.

sections.title: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and with density

parts.title: The weight of the liquid above
parts.html:
At a point in a liquid, the pressure due to the liquid is produced by the weight of the liquid above that point. Deeper means a taller column of liquid above, which weighs more, so the pressure is greater: a dam is built thicker at the bottom, where the pressure is largest; water jets out further from a hole low in a can than from one near the top (June 2025 Q1(d): the force below a bigger or deeper hole is greater); a diver's ears hurt as she descends. Denser liquid means the same column has more mass, so more weight, so more pressure: at the same depth, sea water (1030 kg/m³) presses harder than fresh water (1000 kg/m³), and mercury (13 600 kg/m³) harder still.

The June 2022 report (Q4(c), a graph of pressure against depth for fresh water, asked how the line for sea water would differ): "increasing the density increases the pressure" — the line is steeper (a larger gradient), still straight (pressure proportional to depth), and starts from the same intercept, the atmospheric pressure at the surface. Those four points were the four marks.

The force on each square metre of the wall (force = pressure × area) is therefore largest at the bottom, so the wall must be thickest there to withstand it.

Either way the pressure rises — which is why dams are thicker at the bottom and why water from a lower hole jets out further.

sections.title: The liquid-column equation, and the difference in pressure between two depths

parts.title: Where it comes from, and the trap
parts.html:
A column of liquid of height $h$ and cross-section $A$ has volume $hA$, mass $\rho h A$ and weight $\rho h A g$; spread over the area $A$ at the bottom that is a pressure of $\rho h g$ — the area cancels, so the pressure depends only on depth, density and $g$: $P = h \rho g$. Pressure (Pa) = height (m) × density (kg/m³) × $g$ (10 N/kg). This is the pressure due to the liquid; the total pressure at that depth adds the atmospheric pressure on the surface. The difference in pressure between two depths is $\Delta P = \Delta h \rho g$ with $\Delta h$ the difference in depth — the atmosphere cancels out.

The June 2025 report (Q1(a)(i), finding a height from a pressure): most candidates rearranged correctly, but some used 10 for the density of water rather than $10^3$, and got 35 m for the depth of a pool — "the height of a large building". The examiners' advice: "look at the result of a calculation to see if the value makes sense". The sense check: 10 m of water is about 100 kPa, one atmosphere; a swimming pool is 1–3 m, so 10–30 kPa; the deepest ocean, 11 km, about 110 MPa.

steps: $P = h \rho g$, so $h = P \div (\rho g) = 35\,000 \div (1000 \times 10)$.
$h = 3.5$ m — a sensible depth for a pool. (With $\rho = 10$ the answer would be 350 m: the 2025 mistake.)

sections.title: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced; floating and sinking

parts.title: Where upthrust comes from, and what decides floating
parts.html:
Why there is an upthrust (15.15P): pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the pressure on the bottom face of a submerged object is greater than on its top face. The forces on the sides cancel, but the upward force on the bottom is larger than the downward force on the top, leaving a resultant upward force: the upthrust. It acts on anything in a fluid — partly or fully immersed, in a liquid or a gas (a helium balloon is pushed up by the air).

How big it is (15.16P): the upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object — the weight of the fluid that would have filled the space the object takes up. A 1 m³ block fully under water displaces 1000 kg of water, so the upthrust is 10 000 N whatever the block is made of. So an object weighed in air and then in water seems to lose weight: the loss is the upthrust, which is the weight of water displaced (the June 2025 Q9(a) chain).

Floating and sinking (15.17P): an object floats when the upthrust equals its weight. It sinks into the fluid until it has displaced fluid weighing as much as itself; if that happens before it is fully under, it floats with the rest above the surface; if even fully immersed the displaced fluid weighs less than the object, upthrust < weight and it sinks. In terms of density: an object less dense than the fluid floats (it can displace its own weight of fluid with only part of its volume); one denser sinks. A steel ship floats because the hull and the air inside it together are less dense than water — its shape displaces a large volume. The June 2022 report (Q3(c), a wood sample in water): "wood is less dense than water and would float" scored, but the second mark, "less water would be displaced" (than the wood's own volume), was rarely given.

steps: (a) The upthrusts are equal: the ball floats in both, so in each case the upthrust equals the weight of the ball (June 2023 Q6(c)(i)).
(b) Floating: the weight of the ball = the weight of water displaced.
Sea water is more dense than fresh water…
…so a smaller volume of sea water has the same weight, so less sea water needs to be displaced to support the ball, and less of the ball is below the surface (Q6(c)(ii)).

  • The upward force on the bottom is larger than the downward force on the top, giving a resultant upward force — the upthrust.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
DistortionA change in the shape of an object (stretching, compressing or bending) caused by forces."breaking"
Elastic distortionA distortion that is reversed when the forces are removed: the object returns to its original shape and size."it stretches"
Inelastic distortionA distortion that is permanent: the object does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed."plastic" on its own
ExtensionThe increase in length of a spring: stretched length − original length.the length of the spring
Spring constantThe force needed per unit extension, $k = F \div x$, in N/m — a measure of the spring's stiffness."how springy it is"
Hooke's lawThe extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality: $F = kx$."force = extension"
Limit of proportionalityThe point on a force–extension graph beyond which the line is no longer straight: extension stops being proportional to force.confusing with breaking point
Elastic limitThe point beyond which a spring no longer returns to its original length when unloaded (its distortion becomes inelastic)."where it snaps"
Pressure (Physics only)The force per unit area acting at right angles to a surface: $P = F \div A$, in pascals (N/m²)."force"
Fluid (Physics only)A liquid or a gas: a substance that can flow and takes the shape of its container."a liquid" only
Atmospheric pressure (Physics only)The pressure exerted by the weight of the air above a surface; about 100 kPa at sea level, decreasing with height."air"
Upthrust (Physics only)The upward force on an object in a fluid, caused by the pressure being greater on its lower surface than its upper; equal to the weight of fluid displaced."the object being light"
Floating (Physics only)An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight — it displaces its own weight of fluid before being fully immersed (it is less dense than the fluid)."it is light"

sections.title: Planning the spring practical: the 6-mark method and the seven steps

parts.title: The seven steps for a spring
parts.html:
StepHow does the extension of a spring depend on the force applied?
1 Variablesindependent: the force (the weight hung on the spring); dependent: the extension; control: the same spring, loads added one at a time without jerking, the same ruler
2 Relationship$F = k x$: force proportional to extension (within the limit); a graph of force against extension should be a straight line through the origin with gradient $k$
3 Changehang 100 g masses one at a time: 1 N, 2 N, … up to 6 N or more (at least six values, evenly spaced)
4 Measurethe position of a pointer on the bottom of the spring against a vertical mm ruler, with no load and with each load; extension = reading − no-load reading; force = weight of the masses ($W = mg$)
5 Useplot force against extension; a straight line through the origin shows Hooke's law; the gradient is the spring constant; the area under the line to any extension is the work done stretching the spring
6 Accuracyread the pointer at eye level (no parallax); clamp the ruler vertical and the stand to the bench; let the spring settle before reading; stay below the elastic limit (check the spring returns to its no-load reading); wear eye protection
7 Repeatrepeat the readings while unloading (and again) and take a mean extension for each force

In the 2022–2025 Paper 2H series read for this page the spring practical was not the 6-mark method question, but its parts were marked: the 2023 three marks for two readings and a subtraction, and the 2023 accuracy mark for a change that locates the end of the spring and how it is used ("ignore unqualified references to accuracy or precision" — say what the pointer or eye-level reading prevents: parallax).

parts.title: The 6-mark method
parts.question: Describe an investigation to find the spring constant of a spring. (6 marks)
steps: Clamp the spring from a stand with a metre ruler (mm) clamped vertically beside it and a pointer fixed to the bottom of the spring; read the pointer's position with no load.
Hang a 100 g mass (1.0 N) on the spring, let it settle, and read the pointer again; extension = reading − no-load reading.
Add masses one at a time to at least 6 N, recording the extension for each force.
Read the pointer at eye level to avoid parallax; check the spring returns to the no-load reading when unloaded so that the elastic limit was not passed.
Plot force against extension: a straight line through the origin shows the extension is proportional to the force.
The spring constant is the gradient of the line ($k = F \div x$ with $x$ in metres); repeat while unloading and use the mean.

5UsePlot force against extension; straight line through the origin confirms Hooke's law; gradient = spring constant; area = work done.
6AccuracyRead at eye level with a pointer (no parallax); ruler vertical; let the spring settle; stay below the elastic limit.
7RepeatRepeat on unloading and take a mean extension for each force.
  • Any six of the seven points.

questions.text: Which accuracy statement would the 2023 examiners credit?
options: Use a pointer on the spring and read it at eye level so there is no parallax error
questions.explain: Say what the change is and what it prevents; unqualified 'accuracy' is ignored.

questions.text: A student records the length of the spring for each load and plots force against length. Explain what is wrong and how the spring constant can still be found. (2)
questions.model:
• Hooke's law is about the extension, so force against length does not pass through the origin: the gradient is still $k$ (each extra newton adds the same extra length)…
  • …but to get extensions, subtract the no-load length from every reading and replot (or read $k$ from the gradient of the force–length line directly).

questions.text: Why are readings also taken while the masses are removed one at a time?
options: To check the spring returns to its original length (no inelastic distortion) and to give repeat readings for a mean
questions.explain: Unloading readings are the repeat and the elastic-limit check.

questions.text: In the practical, six 100 g masses stretch the spring from a pointer reading of 215 mm to 275 mm. Taking $g = 10$ N/kg, calculate the spring constant.

checklist: Plan the investigation with the seven steps: variables, relationship, change, measure, use, accuracy, repeat
Say how the result is used: plot force against extension, straight line through the origin, gradient = spring constant, area = work done
Write a 6-mark method from the plan
sections.blurb: A method question on the spring practical wants named apparatus, the two readings that make an extension, a range of loads, the graph and what to take from it, and one accuracy point. The seven steps give all of it in order; the trap is to describe measuring the length rather than the extension.

sections.title: Pressure calculations the hard way: total area, square millimetres, force from pressure, and pressure differences

parts.title: Four papers, four traps
parts.html:
TrapWhat the examiners sawWhat to do
Total areaJune 2022 Q4(a)(i): "the most common mistake was not correctly calculating the area as 4 × area of one hoof" (1 of 2 marks)count the contacts: four hooves, two feet, three legs of a stool; area = $n \times$ one
mm² and cm²June 2025 Q1(c): forgetting to convert mm² to m² gave "an answer that was a million times too large" (1 of 2)square the length conversion: 1 mm = $10^{-3}$ m so 1 mm² = $10^{-6}$ m²; 1 cm² = $10^{-4}$ m²
RoundingJune 2024 Q4(b): substitution (1), evaluation 576 N (1), rounded to 2 s.f. 580 N (1)when the question says "to 2 significant figures", the rounding is a mark on its own
DifferenceJune 2023 Q4(a)(i)–(ii): net pressure $80\,000 - 23\,000 = 57\,000$ Pa; the force of the cabin air on the window used 80 000 (substituting 57 000 there earned only the substitution mark)read which force the question wants: one side's pressure, or the net

And the explanation version (2022 Q4(a)(ii)): larger area → the weight (force) is spread over a larger area → less pressure. Two marks: the larger area, and the weight spread over it giving less pressure; "mass spread out" earned neither.

parts.title: Four feet and square millimetres
parts.question: An elephant weighs 50 000 N and stands on four feet, each with an area of 1200 cm². A woman weighing 600 N stands on one stiletto heel of area 1.0 cm². Compare the pressures. (4 marks)
steps: Elephant: total area $= 4 \times 1200 = 4800$ cm² $= 0.48$ m².
The heel exerts about 60 times the pressure of the elephant, because its force acts on a far smaller area.

questions.text: A table weighs 320 N and stands on four legs. Each leg has a base of area 16 cm². Calculate the pressure on the floor.
A nail is hit with a force of 50 N. The point of the nail has an area of 0.25 mm². Calculate the pressure at the point, in Pa.
The air inside a car tyre is at 250 kPa and the atmospheric pressure outside is 100 kPa. The inner end of the tyre valve has an area of $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ m². Calculate the net force on the valve.
A pressure of $2.3 \times 10^{5}$ Pa acts on a surface of area $3.1 \times 10^{-3}$ m². Calculate the force, to 2 significant figures.
Explain why a tractor with wide tyres can drive over soft ground that a car with narrow tyres would sink into. (3)
questions.model:
• The wide tyres have a much larger area in contact with the ground.
  • The tractor's weight (force) is spread over this larger area.
  • Pressure = force ÷ area, so the pressure on the ground is smaller and the ground is not pushed in as far.

checklist: Use the total contact area: number of feet, legs or tyres × the area of one
Convert cm² and mm² to m² (squared conversions) before substituting
Use $F = PA$, and a pressure difference when there is fluid on both sides
sections.blurb: $P = F/A$ is easy until the area is in the wrong unit, split over four feet, or on both sides of a surface. The four papers' errors: forgetting to multiply by four hooves (2022), leaving mm² in (2025 — a million times out), not rounding to two significant figures when asked (2024), and using the pressure difference where the question wanted the force of the cabin air alone (2023).

sections.title: Pressure–height and pressure–depth graphs: describing, comparing and reading them
equations: \text{depth: a straight line rising from atmospheric pressure}

parts.title: The two graphs and their marks
parts.html:
Pressure against height (atmosphere)Pressure against depth (liquid)
Shapea curve falling: non-linear, the gradient becomes less steep with heighta straight line rising: linear, pressure proportional to depth (plus the constant atmosphere)
Whyless air above → less weight → lower pressure; and the air is less dense higher up, so each km removes less weightthe weight of the column of liquid above grows in proportion to its height; the liquid's density does not change with depth
Interceptabout 100 kPa at sea levelatmospheric pressure at the surface (depth 0), the same whatever the liquid
Marks seen2023 Q4(b): decrease with height (1), non-linear (1), use of numerical data (1); 2024 Q4(c): decreases as height increases / negative correlation (1), non-linear — curved, not proportional, gradient changes (1); a reading within a range; a percentage change2022 Q4(c): density up → pressure up (1), steeper gradient (1), still linear (1), same intercept, the air pressure (1)

Percentage change (2024 Q4(c)(iii)): (new − old) ÷ old × 100 — the scheme gave one mark for the substitution and one for the evaluation, and only one mark for dividing by the new value instead. Reading a graph: say the two values you read and show the subtraction; a reading within the scheme's range scores even if the line is hard to read.

parts.title: Fresh water and sea water on one graph
parts.question: The graph shows total pressure against depth for fresh water and sea water. Describe the two lines and explain the differences and similarities. (4 marks)
steps: Both lines are straight: the pressure increases in proportion to the depth, because the weight of liquid above grows with the height of the column.
Both start at 100 kPa at the surface — the atmospheric pressure, which is the same whatever the liquid.
The sea-water line is steeper (306 kPa against 300 kPa at 20 m): sea water is denser, so the same column has more weight.
At any depth the sea-water pressure is higher by the extra weight of the denser column above — only 6 kPa at 20 m, because the densities differ by just 3 %.

graph.alt: Total pressure against depth: two straight lines from 100 kPa at the surface, fresh water reaching 300 kPa at 20 m and sea water slightly steeper, reaching 306 kPa.

questions.text: Use the graph of total pressure against depth.

parts.text: Read the total pressure at a depth of 10 m in fresh water.
parts.hint: Read up from 10 m to the lower line.
walkthrough: At 10 m the fresh-water line is at 200 kPa.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in total pressure from the surface to 20 m in fresh water.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Why do both lines start at 100 kPa rather than at zero?
options: Because the atmosphere presses on the surface of the water: the total pressure at depth 0 is atmospheric pressure
parts.explain: The intercept is the air pressure.
parts.label: c

graph.alt: Total pressure against depth: two straight lines from 100 kPa at the surface, fresh water reaching 300 kPa at 20 m and sea water slightly steeper, reaching 306 kPa.

questions.text: Describe the difference between a graph of pressure against height in the atmosphere and a graph of pressure against depth in a lake. (3)
questions.model:
• Height: the pressure decreases as height increases; depth: the pressure increases with depth.
  • Height: the graph is non-linear (a curve, less steep higher up, because the air is less dense there); depth: the graph is a straight line (pressure proportional to depth, the water's density being constant).
  • Both start from atmospheric pressure, about 100 kPa, at the surface.

questions.text: In 2024 the percentage change in pressure was calculated as $(74 - 104) \div 104 \times 100 = -29$ %. A student who divided by 74 instead…
options: scored one mark (−41 %), because the change must be divided by the original value
was given the benefit of the doubt
questions.explain: Divide by the starting value.

questions.text: A pressure–height graph for the atmosphere is described by a student as 'inversely proportional'. Comment on this. (2)
questions.model:
• The relationship is not inversely proportional in the strict sense (pressure × height is not constant — at zero height the pressure is 100 kPa, not infinite).
  • The accurate description is a negative, non-linear relationship: pressure decreases as height increases and the fall per kilometre gets smaller. (The 2023 scheme, Q4(b)(i), accepted 'inversely proportional' for the non-linear mark "in this context" — a loose way of saying this.)

checklist: Describe the pressure–height graph: direction, non-linear, with numbers from the graph
Describe the pressure–depth graph: straight, proportional increase, intercept = atmospheric pressure
Compare the lines for two liquids: steeper for the denser one, same intercept
sections.blurb: Two graphs that look alike and behave differently. Pressure against height in the atmosphere is a curve: it falls, and falls more slowly as the air thins. Pressure against depth in a liquid is a straight line: it rises in proportion to depth, starting from atmospheric pressure at the surface, and a denser liquid gives a steeper line from the same start.

sections.title: Upthrust the hard way: apparent weight, volume and density, and the floating ball

parts.title: The four-stage chain
parts.html:
StageEquationJune 2025 Q9(a)(ii)
1 loss in weight = upthrust = weight of fluid displacedupthrust $= W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{fluid}}$2 N (one mark); starting from the wrong value (5 N) lost this mark only
2 volume of fluid displaced = volume of the object$V = \text{upthrust} \div (\rho_{\text{fluid}}\, g)$$1.43 \times 10^{-4}$ m³ (one mark)
3 mass of the object from its weight in air$m = W_{\text{air}} \div g$the density equation with the block's weight (one mark)
4 density$\rho = m \div V$$4.9 \times 10^{3}$ kg/m³ (one mark), error carried forward

The report: "partial credit could be obtained by successfully completing each stage", and on the explanation part (Q9(a)(i)) "only a very few candidates correctly linked the loss in weight with the weight of liquid displaced" — the marks were upthrust (1), equal to the weight of liquid displaced (1), and the liquid being more dense than air (1), which is why the object weighs less in the liquid than in air (there is an upthrust from the air too, but it is tiny). The paper's summary: "less confidence was shown in the application of Archimedes' principle".

The floating ball (June 2023 Q6(c)): a ball floating in fresh water and in sea water has the same upthrust in both — equal to its weight, because it floats. The difference is in how much liquid it must displace: sea water is denser, so a smaller volume of it weighs the same as the ball, so less of the ball is under the surface. Three of the four scheme points: weight of ball = weight of water displaced; sea water more dense; smaller volume displaced to produce the same weight.

parts.title: Density from apparent weight
parts.question: A metal block weighs 9.0 N in air and 7.0 N when fully submerged in a liquid of density 1200 kg/m³. $g = 10$ N/kg. Calculate the density of the block. (4 marks)
steps: Upthrust $= 9.0 - 7.0 = 2.0$ N = weight of liquid displaced.
Mass of liquid displaced $= 2.0 \div 10 = 0.20$ kg, so its volume $= 0.20 \div 1200 = 1.67 \times 10^{-4}$ m³ — the block's volume.
Mass of the block $= 9.0 \div 10 = 0.90$ kg.

questions.text: A stone weighs 6.0 N in air and 4.0 N when hanging fully under water (density 1000 kg/m³). $g = 10$ N/kg.

parts.text: State the upthrust on the stone.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the stone.
parts.hint: Upthrust = weight of water displaced; mass $= 2.0 \div 10$; $V = m \div \rho$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the density of the stone.
parts.label: c

questions.text: Explain why an object appears to weigh less when it is hanging in a liquid than when it is hanging in air. (3)
questions.model:
• In the liquid there is an upthrust on the object, which supports part of its weight, so the force on the string is smaller.
  • The upthrust is equal to the weight of liquid displaced by the object.
  • The liquid is much more dense than air, so the liquid displaced weighs far more than the air the object displaced — the upthrust in air is negligible.

questions.text: A wooden block floats in water and then in oil, which is less dense than water. Compare the upthrust on the block in the two liquids, and explain whether more or less of the block is below the surface in the oil. (4)
questions.model:
• The upthrust is the same in both: the block floats, so in each liquid the upthrust equals the block's weight.
  • Floating: the weight of liquid displaced = the weight of the block.
  • Oil is less dense than water…
  • …so a larger volume of oil must be displaced to have the block's weight: more of the block is below the surface in the oil.

questions.text: A student starts the 2025 chain with an upthrust of 5 N (the weight in the liquid) instead of 2 N (the loss in weight). According to the report, this…
options: lost one mark, with the rest carried forward (3 of 4)
questions.explain: Each stage is credited; an error is carried forward.

questions.text: A hot-air balloon has a volume of 2500 m³. The surrounding air has a density of 1.2 kg/m³ and $g = 10$ N/kg. Calculate the upthrust on the balloon.
questions.hint: Upthrust = weight of air displaced $= \rho V g$.
walkthrough: mass of air displaced $= \rho V = 1.2 \times 2500 = 3000$ kg
upthrust $= 3000 \times 10 = 30\,000$ N (the balloon rises if its total weight is less than this)

checklist: Link the apparent loss in weight to the upthrust and to the weight of fluid displaced
Find the volume of an object from the upthrust and the fluid's density, then its density
Explain why the upthrust on a floating object equals its weight whatever the liquid
sections.blurb: The 2025 Archimedes question had four stages and the examiners said candidates rarely linked them: the loss in weight is the upthrust; the upthrust is the weight of fluid displaced; that gives the volume displaced, which is the object's volume; and the object's weight and volume give its density. Each stage is a mark, and each carries forward.

sections.title: Floating and sinking in the mark-scheme words
equations: \text{floats: weight} = \text{upthrust, less dense than the fluid}

parts.title: Two routes, one link
parts.html:
RouteFloatsSinks
Forcesthe object displaces enough fluid for the upthrust to equal its weight before it is fully immersed; the forces balance and it stays at the surfaceeven fully immersed the fluid displaced weighs less than the object: upthrust < weight, a resultant downward force, and it sinks (accelerates down)
Densitythe object is less dense than the fluid, so its own volume of fluid would weigh more than it — it needs to displace less than its own volume (the 2022 second mark)the object is more dense than the fluid: its own volume of fluid weighs less than it, so it cannot displace enough

The June 2022 report (Q3(c)): "most candidates understood that wood is less dense than water and would float" — one mark — but "not many scored a second mark for explaining that less water would be displaced". That second idea is the bridge between the two routes, and a question that says explain wants it. For the force route, say both forces and which is larger; "it is lighter" or "it has air in it" on its own is neither route.

Applications: a steel ship floats because the hull encloses air, so the ship's average density (steel + air) is less than water's and its shape displaces a large volume; load it and it sits lower, displacing more. A submarine floods its tanks with water to increase its weight above the upthrust (sinks), and blows them out with air to reduce it (rises); at a steady depth, weight = upthrust. A hot-air balloon is less dense than the cooler air around it, so the upthrust from the air it displaces exceeds its weight.

parts.title: Why the cork rises
parts.question: A cork is held under water and released. Explain, in terms of forces, what happens and why. (3 marks)
steps: Fully submerged, the cork displaces its own volume of water; the upthrust equals the weight of that water, which is greater than the cork's weight because cork is less dense than water.
So there is a resultant upward force on the cork and it accelerates upwards.
At the surface it rises partly out of the water, displacing less, until the upthrust has fallen to equal its weight — then it floats, with the forces balanced.

questions.text: A plastic ball (density 950 kg/m³) and a glass marble (density 2500 kg/m³) are dropped into water. Explain, in terms of density and the water displaced, why one floats and the other sinks. (3)
questions.model:
• The plastic ball is less dense than water: its own volume of water would weigh more than it, so it needs to displace less than its own volume of water for the upthrust to equal its weight — it floats (95 % submerged).
  • The marble is more dense than water: even fully immersed it displaces only its own volume of water, which weighs less than the marble…
  • …so the upthrust is less than its weight and there is a resultant downward force: it sinks.

questions.text: Explain, in terms of forces, why a solid steel ball sinks in water. (2)
questions.model:
• Even when fully immersed the ball displaces only its own volume of water, and that water weighs less than the ball (steel is denser than water), so the upthrust is less than the weight.
  • There is a resultant downward force, so the ball accelerates downwards — it sinks.

questions.text: A loaded ship sits lower in the water than an empty one because…
options: its weight is greater, so it must displace more water for the upthrust to equal the larger weight
questions.explain: More weight, more water to displace.

questions.text: Describe how a submarine dives and surfaces. (2)
questions.model:
• To dive it lets water into its ballast tanks: its weight increases until it is greater than the upthrust (which stays the same, the volume being fixed), so it sinks.
  • To surface it pumps air into the tanks, pushing the water out: its weight falls below the upthrust and it rises; at a steady depth weight = upthrust.

questions.text: Which answer would NOT earn a floating mark?
options: Wood is less dense than water
The upthrust equals the block's weight
Less water is displaced than the block's own volume
questions.explain: 'Light' is neither a density nor a force comparison.

checklist: Explain floating and sinking by comparing weight with upthrust
Explain floating and sinking by comparing densities, with the displaced-volume link
Apply it to ships, submarines and balloons
sections.blurb: There are two correct ways to explain floating — compare the weight with the upthrust, or compare the object's density with the fluid's — and the marks come from completing whichever you start. The mark the 2022 examiners said was rarely scored is the link between them: a less dense object displaces less than its own volume of fluid to match its weight.

facts.q: Why does distorting an object need more than one force?
facts.a: One force is a resultant and accelerates the whole object; two forces in different directions change its shape.

facts.q: The second force on a spring hung from a clamp?
facts.a: The clamp pulls up while the weight pulls down.

facts.q: The three kinds of distortion?
facts.a: Stretching, compression, bending.

facts.q: Elastic distortion?
facts.a: The object returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed.

facts.q: Inelastic distortion?
facts.a: Permanent — the object does not return to its original shape.

facts.q: Elastic limit?
facts.a: The point beyond which the spring no longer returns to its original length when unloaded.

facts.q: Hooke's law as an equation?
facts.a: $F = kx$: force = spring constant × extension (extension in m, k in N/m).

facts.q: What does the spring constant tell you?
facts.a: The force per metre of extension — stiffness; unit N/m.

facts.q: x in $F = kx$ is…
facts.a: The extension (change in length), not the length; in metres.

facts.q: 6.2 mm in metres?
facts.a: $6.2 \times 10^{-3}$ m (1600 N instead of 1.6 N lost a mark in 2023).

facts.q: Energy stored in a stretched spring?
facts.a: $E = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$, extension in metres; also the area under the F–x line.

facts.q: Why the ½ in $E = 	frac{1}{2} k x^2$?
facts.a: The force grows from zero to $kx$ as it stretches, so the average force is half the final force.

facts.q: Double the extension: energy stored?
facts.a: Four times — $E \propto x^2$.

facts.q: A linear force–extension graph through the origin shows…
facts.a: Force is directly proportional to extension (Hooke's law); gradient = k.

facts.q: Beyond the limit of proportionality?
facts.a: The graph curves (non-linear): extension no longer proportional to force; each extra newton gives more extension.

facts.q: A rubber band's force–extension graph?
facts.a: A curve from the start — it does not obey Hooke's law.

facts.q: Spring practical: how is the extension measured?
facts.a: Pointer position on a vertical mm ruler with no load and with the load; subtract (2023: three marks).

facts.q: Spring practical: accuracy points?
facts.a: Read at eye level with a pointer (parallax); ruler vertical; let it settle; stay below the elastic limit; repeat unloading.

facts.q: From the force–extension graph of the practical?
facts.a: Gradient = spring constant; area under the line = work done stretching.

facts.q: How to check the elastic limit was not passed?
facts.a: Remove the masses and check the pointer returns to the no-load reading.

facts.q: Pressure equation and unit?
facts.a: $P = F \div A$; pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).

facts.q: Large area means…
facts.a: Small pressure for the same force: snowshoes, wide tyres, camel feet.

facts.q: Explaining a camel's feet (2022)?
facts.a: Larger area → weight (force) spread over a larger area → less pressure. 'Mass spread out' did not score.

facts.q: 1 cm² and 1 mm² in m²?
Direction of the force from a fluid on a surface?
facts.a: At right angles (normal) to the surface, towards it.

facts.q: Total pressure at a depth in a liquid?
facts.a: Pressure due to the liquid + atmospheric pressure.

facts.q: Force on a surface from a pressure?
facts.a: $F = PA$; with fluid on both sides, use the difference in pressure.

facts.q: Two windows, same cabin pressure, different sizes?
facts.a: Same pressure, larger force on the larger window.

facts.q: Why does atmospheric pressure fall with height?
facts.a: Less air above → smaller weight of air pressing down; the air is also less dense higher up.

facts.q: Shape of pressure against height?
facts.a: A curve falling: non-linear, the fall per km shrinks as the air thins.

facts.q: Atmospheric pressure at sea level?
facts.a: About 100 kPa — the weight of the air above each m².

facts.q: Marks for describing the height graph (2023, 2024)?
facts.a: Pressure decreases as height increases; non-linear; use numbers from the graph.

facts.q: Why does pressure in a liquid increase with depth?
facts.a: A taller column of liquid above the point has more weight.

facts.q: Why does pressure in a liquid increase with density?
facts.a: The same column of a denser liquid has more mass, so more weight.

facts.q: Sea water on a pressure–depth graph (2022)?
facts.a: Steeper line, still straight, same intercept (atmospheric pressure).

facts.q: Why is a dam thicker at the bottom?
facts.a: The water is deepest there, so the pressure and the force per m² are greatest.

facts.q: Pressure due to a column of liquid?
facts.a: $P = h \rho g$: height × density × g.

facts.q: Difference in pressure between two depths?
facts.a: $\Delta P = \Delta h \rho g$ — the atmosphere cancels.

facts.q: The 2025 density trap?
facts.a: Using 10 instead of 1000 kg/m³ for water gave a 35 m pool; check the result makes sense (10 m of water ≈ 100 kPa).

facts.q: Why is there an upthrust?
facts.a: Pressure increases with depth, so the pressure on the bottom face is greater than on the top: a resultant upward force.

facts.q: Size of the upthrust?
facts.a: Equal to the weight of fluid displaced by the object.

facts.q: Condition for floating?
facts.a: Upthrust = weight: the object displaces its own weight of fluid before it is fully immersed (less dense than the fluid).

facts.q: Why does a steel ship float?
facts.a: Hull plus enclosed air is less dense than water; its shape displaces a large volume, enough to weigh as much as the ship.

facts.q: Answer 100 times too small for k?
facts.a: The extension was left in cm (2025).

facts.q: Length given, extension wanted?
facts.a: Extension = loaded length − unloaded length; convert to m.

facts.q: Where on the graph is the gradient equal to k?
facts.a: Only on the straight (linear) part.

facts.q: Energy past the limit of proportionality?
facts.a: Still the area under the line — a triangle plus a curved strip; count squares.

facts.q: Extension on the y-axis: the gradient is…
facts.a: $1 \div k$.

facts.q: Spring practical: independent and dependent variables?
facts.a: Independent: force (weight added); dependent: extension.

facts.q: Spring practical: expected graph?
facts.a: Force against extension: straight line through the origin, gradient = k.

facts.q: Pressure under four feet?
facts.a: Area = 4 × the area of one foot (2022: forgetting the 4 cost a mark).

facts.q: Area left in mm² in $P = F/A$?
facts.a: Answer a million times too large (2025).

facts.q: 'To 2 significant figures' in a pressure question?
facts.a: The rounding is its own mark (2024: 576 N → 580 N).

facts.q: Percentage change in pressure?
facts.a: (new − old) ÷ old × 100; dividing by the new value scored one mark (2024).

facts.q: Height graph vs depth graph?
facts.a: Height: curve, falling, non-linear. Depth: straight line, rising, intercept = atmospheric pressure.

facts.q: The 2025 Archimedes chain?
facts.a: Loss in weight = upthrust = weight of fluid displaced → volume displaced = object's volume → mass from weight in air → density.

facts.q: Why does an object weigh less in a liquid than in air?
facts.a: Upthrust = weight of liquid displaced; the liquid is much denser than air, so the upthrust is much larger.

facts.q: A ball floating in fresh and in sea water: the upthrusts?
facts.a: Equal — each equals the ball's weight; less sea water needs displacing because it is denser.

facts.q: The 2022 second mark for 'why does wood float'?
facts.a: Less water is displaced than the wood's own volume (because wood is less dense).

facts.q: Sinking in terms of forces?
facts.a: Even fully immersed, upthrust < weight: a resultant downward force.

facts.q: How does a submarine dive?
facts.a: Floods its tanks so its weight exceeds the (unchanged) upthrust.

facts.q: State what is meant by: distortion.
facts.a: A change in the shape of an object (stretching, compressing or bending) caused by forces.

facts.q: State what is meant by: elastic distortion.
facts.a: A distortion that is reversed when the forces are removed: the object returns to its original shape and size.

facts.q: State what is meant by: inelastic distortion.
facts.a: A distortion that is permanent: the object does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed.

facts.q: State what is meant by: extension.
facts.a: The increase in length of a spring: stretched length − original length.

facts.q: State what is meant by: spring constant.
facts.a: The force needed per unit extension, $k = F \div x$, in N/m — a measure of the spring's stiffness.

facts.q: State what is meant by: Hooke's law.
facts.a: The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality: $F = kx$.

facts.q: State what is meant by: limit of proportionality.
facts.a: The point on a force–extension graph beyond which the line is no longer straight: extension stops being proportional to force.

facts.q: State what is meant by: elastic limit.
facts.a: The point beyond which a spring no longer returns to its original length when unloaded (its distortion becomes inelastic).

facts.q: State what is meant by: pressure.
facts.a: The force per unit area acting at right angles to a surface: $P = F \div A$, in pascals (N/m²).

facts.q: State what is meant by: fluid.
facts.a: A liquid or a gas: a substance that can flow and takes the shape of its container.

facts.q: State what is meant by: atmospheric pressure.
facts.a: The pressure exerted by the weight of the air above a surface; about 100 kPa at sea level, decreasing with height.

facts.q: State what is meant by: upthrust.
facts.a: The upward force on an object in a fluid, caused by the pressure being greater on its lower surface than its upper; equal to the weight of fluid displaced.

facts.q: State what is meant by: floating.
facts.a: An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight — it displaces its own weight of fluid before being fully immersed (it is less dense than the fluid).

types.name: Hooke's law
types.method: Force equals spring constant × extension, as long as the spring has not passed its limit of proportionality. The extension is how much longer the spring is than its natural length, not the total length. Put the extension in metres so that k comes out in N/m; to find k or x, divide F by the other one.
commonErrors: Using the stretched length instead of the extension
Leaving the extension in cm or mm, which gives the wrong spring constant
Dividing the extension by the force when finding k

worked.question: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m. Calculate the force needed to stretch it by 0.2 m.
steps: Known: k = 25 N/m, x = 0.2 m. Unknown: F.
F = k × x
F = 5 N

practice.question: A spring in a laboratory has a spring constant of 40 N/m. Calculate the force needed to produce an extension of 0.15 m.
practice.hint: Multiply the spring constant by the extension.
walkthrough: k = 40 N/m, x = 0.15 m, find F.

practice.question: The spring inside a kitchen scale has a spring constant of 500 N/m. A bag of flour compresses it by 0.04 m. Calculate the force the flour exerts on the spring.
practice.hint: F = k × x works for compression as well as stretching.
walkthrough: k = 500 N/m, x = 0.04 m, find F.

practice.question: A force of 8 N stretches a bungee cord model by 16 cm. Calculate the spring constant of the cord in N/m.
practice.hint: Change 16 cm to metres, then rearrange to k = F / x.
walkthrough: F = 8 N, x = 16 cm = 0.16 m, find k.
F = k × x → k = F / x

practice.question: A spring inside a mattress has a spring constant of 2000 N/m. Calculate the compression produced by a force of 30 N. Give your answer in mm.
practice.hint: Rearrange to x = F / k, which gives metres, then change to mm.
walkthrough: k = 2000 N/m, F = 30 N, find x.
F = k × x → x = F / k

practice.question: A 0.6 kg mass is hung from a spring with a spring constant of 120 N/m. Calculate the extension of the spring in cm.
practice.hint: Find the weight first with W = m × g, then use x = F / k and change to cm.

practice.question: A spring has a natural length of 15 cm. When a force of 1.8 N is applied its length becomes 21 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.
practice.hint: Extension = stretched length − natural length; change it to metres, then k = F / x.

types.name: Energy stored in a stretched spring
types.method: The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring is half × spring constant × extension squared. Change the extension to metres, square it, multiply by k, then halve. To find the extension from the energy, divide E by ½ × k and take the square root.
commonErrors: Squaring the extension in cm: change to metres first

worked.question: A spring with a spring constant of 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Calculate the energy stored in the spring.
steps: Known: k = 200 N/m, x = 0.1 m. Unknown: E.
E = ½ × k × x²
E = 1 J

practice.question: The spring in a toy dart launcher has a spring constant of 400 N/m. It is compressed by 0.05 m. Calculate the energy stored in the spring.
practice.hint: Square the compression first, then multiply by ½ × k.
walkthrough: k = 400 N/m, x = 0.05 m, find E.

practice.question: A toy catapult uses an elastic cord with a spring constant of 30 N/m. The cord is stretched by 0.4 m. Calculate the energy stored in the cord.
practice.hint: E = ½ × k × x²; remember to square 0.4.
walkthrough: k = 30 N/m, x = 0.4 m, find E.

practice.question: A spring in a lab has a spring constant of 150 N/m. It is stretched by 8 cm. Calculate the energy stored in the spring.
practice.hint: Change 8 cm to metres before you square it.

practice.question: A stiff spring in a door closer has a spring constant of 6000 N/m. It is compressed by 15 mm. Calculate the energy stored in the spring.
practice.hint: Change 15 mm to metres (divide by 1000), then use E = ½ × k × x².

practice.question: A spring with a spring constant of 20 N/m stores 0.9 J of energy. Calculate the extension of the spring in m.
practice.hint: Rearrange to x² = E / (½ × k), then take the square root.
walkthrough: E = 0.9 J, k = 20 N/m, find x.
E = ½ × k × x² → x² = E / (½ × k)

practice.question: The spring in a retractable pen has a spring constant of 1000 N/m. When fully pressed it stores 0.45 J of energy. Calculate how far the spring is compressed. Give your answer in cm.
practice.hint: Find x² = E / (½ × k), square root it to get metres, then change to cm.

types.name: Reading a force–extension graph
types.method: On a force–extension graph the straight part through the origin is where the spring obeys Hooke's law. Its gradient is the spring constant: pick a point on the line, change the extension to metres and divide the force by it. The area under the line up to a point is the energy stored, a triangle of area ½ × extension × force. Where the line stops being straight is the limit of proportionality.
commonErrors: Taking the gradient with the extension still in cm or mm
Using force / extension at a point on the curved part, beyond the limit of proportionality
Forgetting the ½ when finding the area of the triangle

worked.question: The graph shows how the extension of a spring changes with the force applied. The line is straight up to point P. Use the gradient of the straight part of the graph to determine the spring constant of the spring in N/m.
steps: Choose a point on the straight part: P at (8 cm, 16 N).
Change the extension to metres: 8 cm = 0.08 m.

practice.hint: Find 3 N on the force axis, go across to the line at A and read down to the extension axis.

Reading down from A to the extension axis gives 6 cm.

practice.question: The graph shows how the extension of a spring changes with the force applied. The line is straight up to point L and curves after it. Use the graph to determine the force at which the spring stops obeying Hooke's law.
practice.hint: Hooke's law holds only on the straight part; read the force at L, where the line starts to curve.
walkthrough: The line is straight from the origin up to L and then curves.
Reading across from L to the force axis gives 12 N.
Force at the limit of proportionality = 12 N

practice.hint: The shaded area is a triangle: ½ × base × height, with the extension in metres.
walkthrough: At 10 cm the force is 8 N; 10 cm = 0.1 m.

practice.question: The graph shows the force applied to the small spring from a pen against its extension in mm. Use the gradient of the graph to determine the spring constant in N/m.
practice.hint: Pick a point on the line, change the extension from mm to metres (divide by 1000), then k = F / x.
walkthrough: Point on the line: (40 mm, 10 N)

practice.hint: Read both coordinates of X, change the extension to metres, then area = ½ × extension × force.
walkthrough: X is at (6 cm, 9 N); 6 cm = 0.06 m.

practice.question: The graph shows the force applied to a spring against its extension. A mass hung from the spring produces an extension of 8 cm, marked as point B. Use the graph to find the force, and so calculate the mass hung from the spring.
practice.hint: Read the force at B, then use W = m × g with g = 10 N/kg to find the mass.

The force is the weight of the mass: W = m × g
